source.subject: Biology
source.unit: Unit 1 — Diversity in the Living World
source.source_scope: Only the content printed on PDF page 4: continuation of section 1.1 on newly identified organisms, local and scientific names, identification, nomenclature, ICBN, ICZN, binomial nomenclature and naming rules.

questions.question: According to the page, what happens as people explore new areas and even areas already explored?
options: New organisms continue to be identified
questions.explanation: The page states that new organisms are continuously being identified as areas are explored.
questions.source_text: as we explore new areas, and even old ones, new organisms are continuously being identified

questions.question: Why can local names of plants and animals cause confusion when people communicate across places?
options: They vary from place to place
They are always written in italics
questions.explanation: The text says local names vary between places, even within one country, creating confusion when referring to organisms.
questions.source_text: These local names would vary from place to place, even within a country

questions.question: What is the process of standardising the naming of living organisms so an organism has the same name worldwide called?
questions.explanation: The page defines nomenclature as the process of naming organisms in a standardised way.
questions.source_text: This process is called nomenclature

questions.question: According to the page, nomenclature is possible only when the organism is:
options: Correctly described and linked to its name
questions.explanation: The text says the organism must be correctly described and it must be known which organism the name is attached to; this is identification.
questions.source_text: nomenclature or naming is only possible when the organism is described correctly and we know to what organism the name is attached to. This is identification.

questions.question: The page uses the term identification for knowing:
options: To which organism a name is attached
The local name in every language
questions.explanation: Identification means knowing what organism a name refers to, after correct description.
questions.source_text: we know to what organism the name is attached to. This is identification.

questions.question: Why have scientists established procedures to assign scientific names to known organisms?
options: To make names acceptable to biologists worldwide
To give each place a different local name
To ensure every organism has many names
questions.explanation: The procedures provide scientific names that biologists around the world accept.
questions.source_text: scientists have established procedures to assign a scientific name to each known organism. This is acceptable to biologists all over the world.

questions.question: Which code does the page identify as providing agreed principles and criteria for scientific names of plants?
questions.explanation: The page says plant scientific names are based on principles in the ICBN.
questions.source_text: International Code for Botanical Nomenclature (ICBN)

questions.question: Which code does the page say animal taxonomists have evolved?
questions.explanation: The page names ICZN as the code evolved by animal taxonomists.
questions.source_text: Animal taxonomists have evolved International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN).

questions.question: Which outcome of scientific names is explicitly stated on the page?
options: Each organism has only one name
Every organism has a local name only
A name can be reused for many known organisms
questions.explanation: The text says scientific names ensure that each organism has only one name.
questions.source_text: The scientific names ensure that each organism has only one name.

questions.question: According to the page, which outcomes should a description and scientific name help ensure?
options: People anywhere in the world arrive at the same name
The name has not been used for another known organism
The organism has a different name in each region
questions.explanation: The page says descriptions should lead people worldwide to the same name and ensure that the name has not already been used for another known organism.
questions.source_text: Description of any organism should enable the people (in any part of the world) to arrive at the same name. They also ensure that such a name has not been used for any other known organism.

questions.question: How many components does each scientific name have in the system described on the page?
questions.explanation: The page says each name has a generic name and a specific epithet.
questions.source_text: Each name has two components – the Generic name and the specific epithet.

questions.question: What is the system of naming an organism using two components called?
questions.explanation: A name with two components is called binomial nomenclature.
questions.source_text: This system of providing a name with two components is called Binomial nomenclature.

questions.question: Who is credited on the page with giving the binomial naming system?
questions.explanation: The text attributes this naming system to Carolus Linnaeus.
questions.source_text: This naming system given by Carolus Linnaeus is being practised by biologists all over the world.

questions.question: Which scientific name for mango is given in the page?
questions.explanation: The page gives the mango scientific name as Mangifera indica.
questions.source_text: The scientific name of mango is written as Mangifera indica.

questions.question: In the name Mangifera indica, which word represents the genus according to the page?
questions.explanation: The text explicitly identifies Mangifera as the genus.
questions.source_text: Mangifera represents the genus while indica, is a particular species, or a specific epithet.

questions.question: In Mangifera indica, the word indica is the:
questions.explanation: The page identifies indica as the specific epithet.
questions.source_text: Mangifera represents the genus while indica, is a particular species, or a specific epithet.

questions.question: Which statements about biological names are stated on the page?
options: They are written in italics when printed
They are Latinised or derived from Latin irrespective of origin
They must always be written in capital letters
questions.explanation: The first rule states that biological names are generally Latin, italicised in print, and Latinised or derived from Latin regardless of origin.
questions.source_text: Biological names are generally in Latin and written in italics. They are Latinised or derived from Latin irrespective of their origin.

questions.question: Which component comes first in a biological name, according to the rules on the page?
questions.explanation: The first word represents the genus and the second component denotes the specific epithet.
questions.source_text: The first word in a biological name represents the genus while the second component denotes the specific epithet.

questions.question: How should the two words of a biological name be written by hand, according to the page?
options: Both underlined together as one continuous line
questions.explanation: The page says both words are separately underlined when handwritten.
questions.source_text: Both the words in a biological name, when handwritten, are separately underlined

questions.question: How are biological names indicated in print, according to the page?
options: By placing them in quotation marks
questions.explanation: The page says printed biological names are written in italics.
questions.source_text: or printed in italics to indicate their Latin origin
